title: Epistulae
author: the Younger Pliny
source: Translated by Claude from phi1318.phi001.perseus-lat1, as held by the Perseus Digital Library.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.
availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit the Perseus Digital Library and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

passages.original: ceteri audaces atque etiam magna ex parte adulescentuli obscuri ad declamandum huc transierunt, tam irreverenter et temere, ut mihi Atilius noster expresse dixisse videatur, sic in foro pueros a centumviralibus causis auspicari, ut ab Homero in scholis. Nam hic quoque ut illic primum coepit esse quod maximum est.
passages.english: the rest are bold, and indeed for the most part obscure young men who have crossed over here to declaim, so disrespectfully and rashly that our friend Atilius seems to me to have put it precisely when he said that boys make their start in the forum with cases before the Centumviral court just as they do in the schools with Homer. For here too, as there, they have begun with what is greatest.

passages.original: Habesne quo tali epistulae parem gratiam referas? Habes, si scripseris num aliquis in municipio vestro ex sodalibus meis, num etiam ipse tu hunc luctuosum Reguli librum ut circulator in foro legeris, ἐπάρας scilicet, ut ait Demosthenes, τὴν φωνὴν καὶ γεγηθὼς καὶ λαρυγγίζων.
passages.english: Have you any way to repay a letter like this in kind? You have, if you write whether any of my friends in your town, or even you yourself, has read this mournful book of Regulus aloud in the forum like a street-performer, 'lifting up', no doubt, as Demosthenes says, 'his voice, rejoicing and bawling from the throat'.
passages.notes: The Greek quotation is from Demosthenes, On the Crown; λαρυγγίζων means roughly 'shouting at the top of one's throat'.

passages.original: Quemadmodum magis approbare tibi possum, quanto opere mirer epigrammata tua Graeca, quam quod quaedam Latine aemulari et exprimere temptavi? in deterius tamen. Accidit hoc primum imbecillitate ingenii mei, deinde inopia ac potius, ut Lucretius ait, egestate patrii sermonis.
passages.english: How can I better prove to you how greatly I admire your Greek epigrams than by the fact that I have tried to rival and render some of them in Latin? For the worse, however. This happened first through the weakness of my talent, and then through the poverty, or rather, as Lucretius says, the destitution of our native tongue.

passages.original: Vides quot versibus Homerus, quot Vergilius arma hic Aeneae Achillis ille describat; brevis tamen uterque est quia facit quod instituit. Vides ut Aratus minutissima etiam sidera consectetur et colligat; modum tamen servat. Non enim excursus hic eius, sed opus ipsum est.
passages.english: You see in how many lines Homer describes the arms of Achilles, and in how many Virgil describes those of Aeneas; yet each is brief, because he does what he set out to do. You see how Aratus pursues and gathers together even the tiniest stars; yet he keeps within measure. For this is not a digression of his, but the work itself.
passages.notes: Latin 'hic ... ille' refers to Virgil and Homer respectively; rendered in natural order.

passages.original: Nam plurimum refert, ut Thucydides ait, κτῆμα sit an ἀγώνισμα; quorum alterum oratio, alterum historia est. His ex causis non adducor ut duo dissimilia et hoc ipso diversa, quo maxima, confundam misceamque, ne tanta quasi colluvione turbatus ibi faciam quod hic debeo;
passages.english: For it makes a very great difference, as Thucydides says, whether something is a 'possession [for ever]' or a 'prize-piece [for the moment]'; of these the latter is oratory, the former history. For these reasons I am not induced to confuse and mix together two things that are unlike, and differ for the very reason that they are the greatest [of their kind], lest, thrown into disorder by such a jumble, as it were, I should do there what I ought to do here;
passages.notes: The Latin says 'quorum alterum oratio, alterum historia', in order matching κτῆμα = oratio; most take the sense as κτῆμα = history, ἀγώνισμα = oratory, and I have translated accordingly; literally 'one of which is oratory, the other history'.

passages.original: Scripsit mimiambos tenuiter argute venuste, atque in hoc genere eloquentissime; nullum est enim genus quod absolutum non possit eloquentissimum dici. Scripsit comoedias Menandrum aliosque aetatis eiusdem aemulatus; licet has inter Plautinas Terentianasque numeres.
passages.english: He has written mimiambi with delicacy, wit and charm, and, in this genre, most eloquently; for there is no genre which, if brought to perfection, cannot be called most eloquent. He has written comedies in emulation of Menander and others of the same age; you may count them among those of Plautus and Terence.
passages.notes: Mimiambi: short dramatic sketches in choliambic verse, in the manner of Herodas.

passages.original: Illud etiam me non ut ambitiosum sed tamen iuvat, quod adicis te meque et gratiarum actione et laude celebratos. Est enim, ut Xenophon ait, ἥδιστον ἄκουσμα ἔπαινος, utique si te mereri putes. Vale.
passages.english: This too pleases me, not as a man seeking popularity, but still it pleases me: that you add that you and I have been honoured with both a vote of thanks and praise. For, as Xenophon says, 'praise is the sweetest thing to hear', especially if you think you deserve it. Farewell.

passages.original: Omnis enim advertit, quod eminet et exstat; sed acri intentione diiudicandum est, immodicum sit an grande, altum an enorme. Atque ut Homerum potissimum attingam, quem tandem alterutram in partem potest fugere ἀμφὶ δὲ σάλπιγξεν μέγας οὐρανός ... ἠέρι δʼ ἔγχος ἐκεκλιτο et totum illud οὔτε θαλάσσης κῦμα τόσον βοάᾳ?
passages.english: For everyone notices what stands out and projects; but it must be judged with keen attention whether it is excessive or grand, lofty or monstrous. And to touch on Homer above all: whom, pray, can it escape, in one direction or the other, [what is meant by] 'and round about the great heaven trumpeted' ... 'and his spear leaned on the mist', and that whole passage 'neither does the wave of the sea roar so loud'?
passages.notes: Greek quotations from the Iliad (21.388, 5.356, 14.394). The Greek has scanning errors (σάλπιγξεν for σάλπιγξεν/σάλπιγξε, ἐκεκλιτο for ἐκέκλιτο); translated as intended.

passages.original: Scio, domine, memoriae tuae, quae est bene faciendi tenacissima, preces nostras inhaerere. Quia tamen in hoc quoque indulsisti, admoneo simul et impense rogo, ut Attium Suram praetura exornare digneris, cum locus vacet.
passages.english: I know, my lord, that our requests stay fixed in your memory, which holds most tenaciously to the doing of kindnesses. Yet because you have indulged [me] in this too, I both remind you and earnestly ask that you would deign to honour Attius Sura with a praetorship, since a place is vacant.
passages.notes: "in hoc quoque indulsisti" is compressed; it may mean that the emperor has already granted favours of this kind, or that he has allowed Pliny to remind him. The sense is uncertain.
